title: The screenless week I didn't think I could survive
body: The first morning was the hardest. The phone stayed on the charger. The laptop lid stayed shut. I sat at my kitchen table with a cup of coffee and the silence was so loud I could hear the hum of the refrigerator. That's the lede. The quiet is the first thing you notice. It is not empty. It is full of the small sounds you have been tuning out for years. The clink of the spoon on the ceramic. The scrape of the chair leg on the floor. The real world is not silent. It is just not digital. By day three, the phantom vibrations started. I would check my pocket for a phone that wasn't there. My thumb would twitch, looking for a screen to swipe. This is the withdrawal. The digital itch. You realize how often your fingers move on their own, how many times a day you reach for a distraction without even thinking about it. The habit is the cage. But something else happened. The afternoon light changed. I noticed it because I wasn't staring at a screen. The way it hit the dust motes in the air. The long shadows stretching across the street. I started to see the seasons changing in real time, not through a filter. I saw the neighbor's dog digging a hole under the hydrangea bush. I heard the argument two houses down about a misplaced garbage can. The street started to feel like a place again, not just a backdrop for my digital life. Bottom line up front. This is not about rejecting technology. It's about remembering you have a choice. The screen is a tool. A powerful one. But when it becomes the default, it stops serving you and starts serving itself. It steals your attention, one micro-second at a time. The week ended. The screens came back on. The world rushed back in. But something had shifted. The silence I had feared now felt like a resource I could tap into. The question I'm left with is this. What small, non-digital habit could I build to protect that quiet space for myself, even just for ten minutes a day?
